description: Primary and secondary data collection, storage devices, and how test data proves an IT product works correctly.
hero_keywords: data storage server room hard drives
hero_image_caption: Rows of hard drives in a data centre storing large volumes of collected information.
content_html:
How Data Is Collected

Before an IT system can process or store data, that data must be collected. The spec divides collection methods into two categories. Primary data is gathered directly by the organisation: examples include sending an email survey, conducting an interview and publishing an online questionnaire. Primary data is current and specific to your needs, but it takes time and resources to collect.

Secondary data has already been collected by someone else — examples include books, government statistics, magazines and websites. Secondary data is often free and immediately available, but it may be out of date, biased or not exactly matched to what you need. In an exam scenario, you may need to judge which collection method suits the described context and justify your choice.

Key Fact

Primary data collection methods: email, interview, online questionnaire/survey. Secondary data sources: book, government statistics, magazine, website. Primary data is specific but costly to collect; secondary data is cheap and fast but may be outdated or not tailored to your needs.

Where Collected Data Is Stored

Once data is collected, it must be stored. The spec separates storage into logical location (where the data appears to the user) and physical location (where it actually lives).

Cloud storage is the key logical location: data is stored on remote servers managed by a third-party provider and accessed via the internet. Cloud storage is scalable and accessible from anywhere, but it requires an internet connection and raises data security and privacy concerns.

Physical storage splits into internal and external devices. Internal devices sit inside the computer: the primary hard drive stores the OS, applications and user files; a network drive is a storage device shared across a local network, allowing multiple users to save to a central location. External devices are removable and portable: a portable HDD (hard disk drive) offers large capacity at low cost but is vulnerable to physical damage; a portable SSD (solid-state drive) is faster, lighter and more durable but more expensive per gigabyte; a portable USB flash drive (memory stick) is small and convenient for small files; a network-attached storage (NAS) device connects to a network and provides shared storage without needing a server; a portable wireless drive creates its own Wi-Fi hotspot so multiple devices can connect without cables.

Exam questions often ask you to select a storage option for a given scenario. Think about: capacity (how much data?), portability (does it need to move between locations?), speed (how quickly does it need to be read/written?), cost and security (who else could access it?).

A photographer backing up thousands of RAW image files needs high capacity — a portable HDD or NAS device is suitable. A student saving a single coursework document needs portability — a USB flash drive works. A business with ten employees needing shared access to the same files benefits from cloud storage or a NAS device so everyone accesses the latest version from any device.

Key Fact

There are five named external storage devices: portable HDD, portable SSD, NAS device, portable USB flash drive and portable wireless drive. Each has different capacity, speed, cost and portability characteristics — always match your choice to the scenario’s needs.

Why Testing Matters

Testing is essential because IT products that have not been properly tested can crash, produce incorrect outputs or create security vulnerabilities. The consequences of not testing include data loss, financial damage, reputational harm and, in safety-critical systems (such as hospital equipment or traffic management), potential harm to people. The spec requires you to understand why testing is needed, the effects of not testing, and the advantages and disadvantages of testing.

Test Data

The spec identifies three types of test data. Valid test data is typical data the system should accept. Extreme test data is at the very edge of what is acceptable (e.g. 0 and 100 on a 0–100 scale) — it should be accepted. Invalid (erroneous) test data is data that should be rejected (e.g. −5 on a 0–100 scale, or the word “hello” in an age field).

A common mistake is treating extreme and invalid as the same. They are not: extreme values pass the check (they are valid, just at the boundary); invalid values fail the check. For example, on a ticket booking form where age must be 1–120: valid test data = 25; extreme = 1 and 120; invalid = 0, 121, “twelve”.

Technical testing checks that all functions work as specified — for example, that a formula produces the correct output, that navigation links go to the correct page, and that validation rules reject invalid entries. It is carried out by the developer.

User testing checks that real users can accomplish tasks effectively without confusion. It uncovers usability problems that technical testing misses — for example, a button may work technically but be placed in a position that users find confusing. Feedback from user testing is used to refine the HCI design and improve accessibility.
exam_tip_html: The three types of test data are a frequent source of exam errors. Remember: valid data should be accepted and processed correctly; extreme data is at the boundary but should still be accepted; invalid/erroneous data should be rejected. If a question asks you to “describe” each type, name it and give a specific example linked to the scenario — for instance, if the scenario mentions an age field for a cinema booking system, say “valid: age 25; extreme: age 1 and age 100; invalid: −1 or the word ‘old’”. Avoid vague answers like “a number” without connecting it to the context.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Data can be collected through primary methods (email, interview, online questionnaire — original, specific, costly) or secondary sources (book, government statistics, magazine, website — fast, cheap, possibly outdated).
  • Storage options range from cloud (accessible anywhere, needs internet) through internal devices (primary hard drive, network drive) to five named external devices: portable HDD, portable SSD, NAS device, USB flash drive and portable wireless drive.
  • Test data has three types: valid (should be accepted), extreme (boundary — should be accepted), invalid/erroneous (should be rejected). Technical testing checks functionality; user testing checks usability.

practice_questions.text: On the page, sketch a data flow diagram for a small library that: collects member data via an online registration form; stores it on a network drive; and allows members to search for available books via a website. Include: at least three labelled processes; the storage location; at least two data flows shown with arrows; and a clear connection to the library scenario.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–8): at least three distinct, labelled process boxes (e.g. submit registration form → validate data → store to network drive → search database → display results) (2); storage clearly labelled as network drive or similar (1); at least two directional arrows correctly showing data flow (2); clear labels on all flows (1); visible link to library scenario (member, books, availability) (1); overall completeness and clarity (1).
Secure (5–6): most criteria met; minor omissions in labelling or one missing flow arrow.
Developing (3–4): some labelled processes; arrows present but incomplete or incorrectly directed; limited scenario connection.
Emerging (1–2): minimal attempt, very few labelled elements.
0: no creditworthy attempt.

practice_questions.text: Identify one primary data collection method.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: any one of — email; interview; online questionnaire; online survey. Do not accept book, government statistics, magazine or website (secondary sources).

practice_questions.text: Outline the difference between technical testing and user testing.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks: technical testing checks that all functions work as specified, carried out by the developer (1); user testing checks that real users can accomplish tasks effectively, uncovering usability issues not found in technical testing (1). Award 1 mark if only one type is described accurately.

practice_questions.text: Explain why extreme test data is different from invalid test data. Use an example to support your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (3): extreme data is at the boundary of the acceptable range and should be accepted by the system (1); invalid/erroneous data falls outside the acceptable range or is in the wrong format and should be rejected (1); example: for an age field accepting 1–120, age 1 and age 120 are extreme (accepted), age 0 or age 121 are invalid (rejected) (1).
Secure (2): correct distinction made with a partial example.
Developing (1): identifies that they are different types without explaining how.
Emerging (0): no creditworthy content.

practice_questions.text: Describe two advantages of using cloud storage over a portable USB flash drive for a team of five designers sharing project files.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks, one per advantage: cloud storage allows all five team members to access the latest version from any device with internet access, preventing version conflicts (1); cloud storage is automatically backed up by the provider, reducing the risk of data loss if a physical device is lost or damaged (1). Accept other clearly described advantages linked to the team-sharing context.

practice_questions.text: Describe the purpose of testing an IT product and explain two effects of not testing it before release.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6): clear purpose stated (ensures the product functions correctly and meets requirements before use) (1); effect 1 described and explained with impact (e.g. if navigation links are broken, users cannot access pages, reducing trust in the product and causing loss of revenue for the business) (2); effect 2 described and explained with impact (e.g. validation errors not caught in testing could allow invalid data into the database, corrupting records and causing incorrect outputs such as wrong billing amounts) (2); well-structured, linked reasoning throughout (1).
Secure (3–4): purpose clear; two effects described but explanation of impact is limited.
Developing (2): purpose stated; one effect described without impact.
Emerging (1): vague awareness that testing is important; no specific effects described.
0: no creditworthy content.

knowledge_checks.q: Which of the following is a secondary data source?
Which type of test data sits at the boundary of the acceptable range and should still be accepted by the system?
A _____ storage device connects to a local network and provides shared file storage for multiple users without requiring a dedicated server.
_____ testing is carried out by real users to uncover usability problems that a developer's functional testing cannot detect.
Match each storage type to its key characteristic.
right: Small, convenient, suited to carrying small files between locations
Shared internal storage accessed by multiple users on a local network
Remote servers accessed over the internet from any device
Faster and more durable than a hard disk drive but more expensive per GB

flashcard_questions.q: Name three primary data collection methods.

flashcard_questions.a: Any three of: book, government statistics, magazine, website.
Data stored on remote servers accessed over the internet.
Network-attached storage — provides shared file storage over a local network.
Typical data within the acceptable range that the system should accept.
Data at the boundary of the acceptable range — should be accepted.
Data outside the acceptable range or wrong format — should be rejected.
That all functions work as specified by the developer.
That real users can accomplish tasks effectively without confusion.

flashcard_questions.q: Give one advantage of a portable SSD over a portable HDD.
flashcard_questions.a: Faster read/write speeds and more physically durable.

glossary_terms.definition: Data collected first-hand by the person or organisation that needs it, such as through email, interview or online questionnaire.
Data collected by someone else for a different purpose, which is then used by another organisation, such as data from books, government statistics, magazines or websites.
Remote servers accessed over the internet to store and retrieve data, so files are available from any device with internet access.
Data within the expected and acceptable range that the system should accept and process correctly, used to confirm normal operation.
Data at the boundaries of the acceptable range that the system should still accept — used to test whether boundary conditions are handled correctly.
Data that falls outside the acceptable range or is in the wrong format, which the system should reject, such as a letter entered in a numeric field.
